options.0: A Bernoulli variable takes only the values $0$ and $1$ — it records whether a single trial succeeded. $X$ here can be $5$, or $50$. Ask what values $X$ can actually take.
options.1: A binomial counts successes in a **fixed** number of trials. Here the number of trials is not fixed — it is the thing being counted, and it has no upper bound.
options.3: A Poisson counts events in a fixed interval of time or space, and it can be $0$. Can $X$ be $0$ here? And is there an interval in this question?

feedback.reconsider: Write down the set of values $X$ can take, and whether the number of trials is fixed in advance or is itself the random thing. Those two questions separate all four options.

distractors.0: No. Bernoulli takes values in $\{0,1\}$ only.
distractors.1: No. Binomial fixes $n$ in advance and counts successes; here $n$ is what we are counting.
distractors.3: No. Poisson is supported on $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ and models counts in an interval; $X \ge 1$ always, and there is no interval here.

explanation:
## The answer

$X$ is **geometric** with $p = \tfrac12$:

$$\P(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p = \left(\tfrac12\right)^{k}, \qquad k = 1,2,3,\dots$$

and $\E[X] = 1/p = 2$. On average two tosses, which matches intuition.

## Four questions, four distributions

| the question | distribution | support |
| --- | --- | --- |
| did this one trial succeed? | Bernoulli($p$) | $\{0,1\}$ |
| how many successes in $n$ trials? | Binomial($n,p$) | $\{0,\dots,n\}$ |
| how many trials until the first success? | Geometric($p$) | $\{1,2,\dots\}$ |
| how many events in a fixed interval? | Poisson($\lambda$) | $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ |

Naming the distribution is identifying the question, and the fastest way to do it is to write down the **support** — the set of values the variable can take. Here $X \ge 1$ with no upper bound, which eliminates three of the four immediately.

## The convention to watch

"Geometric" is used for two different variables: the number of **trials** including the success (support $1,2,3,\dots$, mean $1/p$) and the number of **failures** before it (support $0,1,2,\dots$, mean $(1-p)/p$). They differ by one. Textbooks disagree, so say which you mean — this problem says it in the option text for exactly that reason.

## The property that makes it geometric

It is **memoryless**: $\P(X > m + n \mid X > m) = \P(X > n)$. Ten tails in a row do not make a head more likely next. The geometric is the only discrete distribution with that property, and the exponential is the only continuous one.
